# Explicit depth and asymmetry localization of a common cap contact

Let `d>=2`, let K be a d-dimensional convex body of volume W, and let
`y in K`. Consider any finite family of closed halfspaces through y
whose union is all of `R^d`. In particular a strictly positive balanced
circuit of normals has this covering property. Put
\[
 \delta=\operatorname{depth}_K(y)
 =\min_{|u|=1}\frac{|K\cap\{u\cdot(x-y)\ge0\}|}{W},
\]
\[
 B=\max_i\frac{|K\cap H_i|}{W}.
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{\quad B\ge
 \max\{\gamma_d,\ \delta,\ \gamma_{d-1}(1-\delta)\}.\quad}
\tag{1}
\]
Here `gamma_k=(k/(k+1))^k` for positive k. Thus for
`gamma_d<=tau<gamma_(d-1)`, the cap-budget condition `B<=tau` implies
\[
 \boxed{\quad\operatorname{depth}_K(y)
       \ge F_d(\tau):=1-\frac{\tau}{\gamma_{d-1}}>0.\quad}
\tag{2}
\]
This is an explicit affine-invariant localization inside an actual Tukey
depth region. It applies to every finite positive circuit, without
requiring its contact to be a centroid. We do not assert that F_d is
the pointwise best possible universal function.

## 1. Proof by an actual convex truncation

The minimum in the definition of delta is attained: the halfspace mass
is continuous in its unit normal by dominated convergence, since each
limiting hyperplane has d-dimensional volume zero. Also `0<=delta<=1/2`,
because opposite through-y caps have masses summing to W.

Choose a minimizing normal u and let
\[
 G=\{x:u\cdot(x-y)\ge0\},\qquad
 K'=K\cap\{x:u\cdot(x-y)\le0\}.
\]
The retained convex body K' has volume `(1-delta)W>=W/2`. It is a
full-dimensional compact convex body, and y is on its boundary: it
belongs to its supporting plane. This includes delta=0, when the
truncation may remove only a null face and K'=K.

Apply the proved theorem in
`candidate f9c635ce5abe9f17` to K' and the
**same original cap family**. Its members still cover the full ambient
space and all their boundaries still pass through y. Consequently
\[
 \max_i|K'\cap H_i|\ge\gamma_{d-1}(1-\delta)W.
\]
Each truncated intersection is contained in its original intersection,
proving the last lower bound in (1). Independently, the original family
covers the ordinary centroid of K, so one member has volume at least
`gamma_d W` by classical Grünbaum. Every member contains y and thus
has volume at least `delta W`. These give the other two bounds in (1).
Rearrangement proves (2). If all cap masses are strictly less than
`tau W`, the resulting lower bound on delta is strict as well.

No cut changes the point, its membership, or the cap orientations. The
only discarded intersection is the boundary hyperplane, whose ordinary
volume is zero. A proposed budget below gamma_d is impossible already
from the centroid argument. At tau=gamma_(d-1), (2) becomes zero, in
agreement with the exact boundary-contact examples.

## 2. An explicit Minkowski-asymmetry inner body

For `y in int K`, define the affine-invariant inner symmetry ratio
\[
 \rho_K(y)=\max\{\rho\ge0:y-\rho(K-y)\subset K\}.
\tag{3}
\]
It is positive and at most one; put `rho_K(y)=0` on the boundary.
The budget condition from (2) also implies
\[
 \boxed{\quad \rho_K(y)\ge
       \left(\frac{\gamma_{d-1}}{\tau}\right)^{1/d}-1.\quad}
\tag{4}
\]
Equivalently, writing the right side as rho_0, the contact satisfies the
actual set containment `y-rho_0(K-y) subset K`.

To prove it, translate y to zero. For any unit u, let the two support
distances be
\[
 a=-\min_K u\cdot x>0,\qquad b=\max_K u\cdot x>0.
\]
Choose a support point p with `u.p=b`. The homothetic copy
\[
 p+\frac b{a+b}(K-p)
\]
lies in K by convexity and lies on the positive side of the plane
through y by its minimum scalar product. Therefore
\[
 \frac{|K\cap\{u\cdot x\le0\}|}{W}
 \le1-\left(\frac b{a+b}\right)^d.
\]
The left side is at least delta. Combining with (2) gives
`b/(a+b)<= (tau/gamma_(d-1))^(1/d)`, or
`a/b>=(gamma_(d-1)/tau)^(1/d)-1`. This holds in every direction.
The support-function description of `-rho K subset K` says exactly
that rho is at most every ratio a/b (the opposite direction gives the
equivalent b/a ratios). Thus it proves (4).

This proof gives also the standalone location bound
\[
 B\ge\frac{\gamma_{d-1}}{(1+\rho_K(y))^d},
\]
although (1), expressed by the actual depth, is at least as strong.
The exponent d in the supporting-direction volume estimate is exact
for a cone cut parallel to its base; no ambient or projected measure is
substituted for ordinary volume.

## 3. Exact calibration and limits of the claimed sharpness

At a boundary contact, delta=0, and the sharp pyramid example from the
dimension-drop theorem has every cap fraction exactly gamma_(d-1).
Thus (1) is exact at that endpoint. At the centroid of a d-simplex,
delta=gamma_d and its d+1 canonical centroid vertex caps cover space
with every fraction gamma_d; (1) is exact there as well. At the center
of a centrally symmetric body, delta=1/2, and two opposite through-center
halfspaces both have fraction one half, attaining the delta term.

For example, in dimension two the explicit implication is
`depth_K(y)>=1-2 tau` for `4/9<=tau<1/2`; at the smallest permitted
budget it guarantees depth at least one ninth. In dimension three it
is `depth_K(y)>=1-(9/4)tau` for `27/64<=tau<4/9`, giving at least
`13/256` at tau=27/64.

These exact endpoint tests do **not** prove that the linear term in
(2) is optimal at every intermediate budget. The argument supplies a
proved numerical function and an actual inner containment, rather than
an unspecified compactness modulus or a complete stability theorem.

## 4. Full-rank circuits and exact rigidity at the smallest budget

Two further exact consequences sharpen the endpoint information.

**Circuit rank.** If every cap in the cover has fraction strictly less
than `gamma_(d-1)`, then every minimal positive dependence among its
normals uses exactly `d+1` normals and has rank d. In particular the
family contains a full-rank positive circuit.

To see existence, write the halfspaces as
`H_i={x:u_i.(x-y)>=0}`, with all u_i nonzero. If zero were outside
the convex hull of these finitely many normals, strict separation
would give a vector v with `u_i.v<0` for every i. Then `y+v` would
belong to none of the halfspaces, contradicting the cover. Select a
subset minimal for containing zero in its convex hull. Its positive
convex dependence has strictly positive coefficients, and minimality
forces affine independence of the selected normals: if they had
an affine dependence, subtract a suitable multiple
from the positive coefficients to make one coefficient zero without
making any negative or changing their sum. Their affine hull contains
zero, so its dimension equals their linear rank r. Their cardinality
is therefore r+1 (and their unique linear dependence is positive).

If r<d, the common boundary flat `y+ker(u_i)_i` contains a point
outside K because K is bounded. The same circuit caps have all their
boundaries through that exterior point and still cover space, by
their positive dependence. The dimension-drop theorem would force
one cap fraction at least `gamma_(d-1)`, a contradiction. Therefore
r=d and the circuit has d+1 members. This argument also proves the
claim for every minimal positive dependence in the original family.

**Smallest-budget rigidity.** If every cap in the cover has fraction
at most `gamma_d`, its common contact y is the ordinary centroid g
of K. Consequently its ordinary depth is at least gamma_d, improving
(2) at this single endpoint to the exact value `F_d(gamma_d)=gamma_d`.

Indeed, gamma_d is strictly smaller than gamma_(d-1), so select the
full-rank positive circuit just proved. If g lay strictly inside one
of its caps, moving that cap's boundary parallel to itself until it
passes through g would strictly remove positive volume: g lies in
the interior of K, so the intervening open slab meets an interior
ball. The through-g cap has volume at least `gamma_d W` by Grünbaum,
contradicting the original budget. Hence
`u_i.(g-y)<=0` for every selected normal. Multiplying by its strictly
positive balancing coefficients and summing yields zero. Each term
therefore vanishes. Full rank now forces `g=y`.

The ordinary centroid belongs to the interior of a full-dimensional
convex body: a boundary supporting functional would have strict
one-sided inequality on a positive-volume interior subset, so its
mean could not equal the boundary value. This justifies the strict
slab-removal step above without any smoothness assumption. The proof
does not use the classification of equality bodies in Grünbaum's
inequality, and makes no continuity claim for the best possible
localization function as tau approaches gamma_d from above.
